verses.text: Now after these things, in the reign of Artaxerxes king of Persia, Ezra the son of Seraiah, the son of Azariah, the son of Hilkiah,
the son of Shallum, the son of Zadok, the son of Ahitub,
the son of Amariah, the son of Azariah, the son of Meraioth,
the son of Zerahiah, the son of Uzzi, the son of Bukki,
the son of Abishua, the son of Phinehas, the son of Eleazar, the son of Aaron the chief priest —

this Ezra went up from Babylon. He was a skilled scribe in the law of Moses, which Yahweh, the God of Israel, had given; and the king granted him all his request, according to Yahweh his God’s hand on him.
Some of the children of Israel, including some of the priests, the Levites, the singers, the porters, and the temple servants went up to Jerusalem in the seventh year of Artaxerxes the king.
He came to Jerusalem in the fifth month, which was in the seventh year of the king.
For on the first day of the first month he began to go up from Babylon; and on the first day of the fifth month he came to Jerusalem, according to the good hand of his God on him.
For Ezra had set his heart to seek Yahweh’s law, and to do it, and to teach statutes and ordinances in Israel.
Now this is the copy of the letter that the king Artaxerxes gave to Ezra the priest, the scribe, even the scribe of the words of Yahweh’s commandments, and of his statutes to Israel:
Artaxerxes, king of kings, To Ezra the priest, the scribe of the law of the perfect God of heaven. Now
I make a decree, that all those of the people of Israel, and their priests and the Levites, in my realm, who intend of their own free will to go to Jerusalem, go with you.
Because you are sent by the king and his seven counselors, to inquire concerning Judah and Jerusalem, according to the law of your God which is in your hand,
and to carry the silver and gold, which the king and his counselors have freely offered to the God of Israel, whose habitation is in Jerusalem,

and all the silver and gold that you will find in all the province of Babylon, with the freewill offering of the people, and of the priests, offering willingly for the house of their God which is in Jerusalem;

therefore you shall with all diligence buy with this money bulls, rams, lambs, with their meal offerings and their drink offerings, and shall offer them on the altar of the house of your God which is in Jerusalem.
Whatever seems good to you and to your brothers to do with the rest of the silver and the gold, do that according to the will of your God.
The vessels that are given to you for the service of the house of your God, deliver before the God of Jerusalem.
Whatever more will be needed for the house of your God, which you may have occasion to give, give it out of the king’s treasure house.

I, even I Artaxerxes the king, make a decree to all the treasurers who are beyond the River, that whatever Ezra the priest, the scribe of the law of the God of heaven, requires of you, it shall be done with all diligence,
up to one hundred talents  of silver, and to one hundred cors  of wheat, and to one hundred baths  of wine, and to one hundred baths of oil, and salt without prescribing how much.
Whatever is commanded by the God of heaven, let it be done exactly for the house of the God of heaven; for why should there be wrath against the realm of the king and his sons?
Also we inform you that it shall not be lawful to impose tribute, custom, or toll, on any of the priests, Levites, singers, porters, temple servants, or laborers of this house of God.

You, Ezra, according to the wisdom of your God that is in your hand, appoint magistrates and judges, who may judge all the people who are beyond the River, who all know the laws of your God; and teach him who doesn’t know them.

Whoever will not do the law of your God and the law of the king, let judgment be executed on him with all diligence, whether it is to death, or to banishment, or to confiscation of goods, or to imprisonment.
Blessed be Yahweh, the God of our fathers, who has put such a thing as this in the king’s heart, to beautify Yahweh’s house which is in Jerusalem;

and has extended loving kindness to me before the king and his counselors, and before all the king’s mighty princes. I was strengthened according to Yahweh my God’s hand on me, and I gathered together chief men out of Israel to go up with me.

footnotes.content: Here begins a long genealogy traced back to Aaron himself. When the Scripture lingers over names like this, it's telling us something matters: this man Ezra carries the weight of a faithful line. The Lord preserves His people not in isolation but in families, generations reaching back to those who served Him truly.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Another step down through history—Zadok is there, the priest who remained faithful when others wavered. These names are not mere lists but proof that faithfulness echoes down through the years. God remembers the righteous, and His work continues through their descendants.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Azariah appears twice in this chain—a name meaning "the Lord helps." What a reminder in the middle of genealogy that every ancestor who bore this lineage did so because the Lord helped them. Our own stories, too, are upheld by His hand if we will see it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The line continues, unbroken through exile and return. Zerahiah, Uzzi, Bukki—each name a link forged by the Lord's faithfulness, not their own strength. In our own lives, we inherit blessing not because we're special but because we're grafted into a story of God's patient mercy.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The line runs all the way back to Aaron, the chief priest—Ezra stands in the priestly succession itself. This isn't accidental. God designed His people to remember their spiritual forebears, to know themselves part of something older and larger than their own generation. We, too, inherit a priesthood through Jesus.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Skilled scribe in the law of Moses"—Ezra studied deeply, then moved as the Lord's hand guided him. Notice how the text credits both his diligence and God's favor: "the king granted him all his request, according to Yahweh his God's hand." Preparation and prayer, then trust. That's the pattern.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A mixed company went up—priests, Levites, singers, porters, temple servants. Not the elite alone. God gathers people of all stations to rebuild His house. Each role mattered: some for worship, some for service, all needed. We forget this when we measure ourselves against others.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They arrived in the fifth month—a specific moment in time preserved in memory. The Lord's work isn't vague or hurried. He marks the day, counts the journey, honors the arrival. When we set our hearts to serve Him, He notices when we finally get there.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: From the first month to the fifth month—a four-month journey preserved in the annals. Ezra attributes their safe passage to "the good hand of his God on him." Protection and provision came not by military might but by the Lord's active favor. Anyone traveling knows that four months of safety in ancient roads is answered prayer.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Set his heart to seek Yahweh's law, and to do it, and to teach it." Three movements: seek, do, teach. A grandparent sees this and knows: this is what integrity looks like. Ezra didn't study for status or power—he studied to live rightly and show others the way. The Lord can work through such a person.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A copy of the king's letter follows—Artaxerxes grants permission and resources. What strikes me is that pagans could see something worth honoring in Ezra's devotion. His character preceded his words. Sometimes our witness to faith isn't what we say but what others observe in how we live.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Artaxerxes, king of kings"—he names his titles first, then addresses Ezra. Yet the letter's real power lies not in the king's authority but in his openness to "the perfect God of heaven." Even rulers sense when they've met something larger than themselves.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "All those of the people of Israel... who intend of their own free will to go to Jerusalem." Not forced, not compelled—chosen. The king grants freedom of conscience. What pagan wisdom that was! Yet it mirrors something deeper: the Lord never forces His people. He invites, and those who love Him choose to return.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Ezra goes as inspector and teacher both—"to inquire concerning Judah and Jerusalem, according to the law of your God." His mission binds official authority with spiritual authority. God can use unlikely circumstances to advance His kingdom when His people are faithful and alert.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The king and his counselors "have freely offered to the God of Israel, whose habitation is in Jerusalem." A pagan ruler gives to the God of Israel—not worship, perhaps, but recognition and honor. When we live faithfully, the world's response is often more generous than we expect.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Silver and gold from Babylon—the very place of exile. What a reversal: the kingdom that once carried Israel away now sends provision for Israel to rebuild. The Lord's reversals are often slow, but they are sure. What seemed like the end becomes a doorway.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Buy bulls, rams, lambs, with their meal offerings and drink offerings, and offer them on the altar." The sacrificial system continues even after exile. These animals, these offerings—they are visible reminders that sin requires atonement, that we cannot approach God on our own merit. Every sacrifice pointed ahead to the Lamb without blemish.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Whatever seems good to you and to your brothers to do with the rest... do that according to the will of your God." The king gives both resources and liberty. Ezra is trusted to discern the Lord's will. That's no small grant—it means the king believes a man can know and follow the mind of God.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "The vessels that are given to you for the service of the house of your God, deliver before the God of Jerusalem." Sacred objects returned to sacred use—a restoration of what was broken. The house of God would have working vessels again. Redemption often looks like this: lost things made whole.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Out of the king's treasure house"—imperial wealth flows to rebuild the house of God. History remembers kings for monuments and military victories, but here Artaxerxes's legacy is that he funded another nation's temple. In God's eyes, that counts as greatness.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "I, even I Artaxerxes the king, make a decree"—the repetition shows solemnity and finality. The treasurers beyond the River are bound by the king's word to grant Ezra what he needs. Authority given to serve God's work. What a peculiar power, used rightly.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: One hundred talents of silver, one hundred cors of wheat, wine, oil—amounts listed with precision. Material abundance for material work. The rebuilding was no spiritual abstraction; it required real resources, real labor, real sacrifice. God meets us in the concrete world, not only in heaven.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Whatever is commanded by the God of heaven, let it be done exactly... for why should there be wrath against the realm?" Even a pagan king fears the anger of the God of heaven. There's a deep wisdom here: recognize the Lord's authority, and you gain peace; resist it, and you invite judgment.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The priests, Levites, singers, and servants are exempt from taxes and levies. A people at work for God's house need freedom from financial burden. The principle holds: when we serve the Lord, He provides what we need and guards our focus from distraction.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "According to the wisdom of your God that is in your hand, appoint magistrates and judges." Ezra gains judicial authority because he carries God's law. His appointment is based not on lineage alone but on his studied knowledge and integrity. God equips those who genuinely seek Him.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Judgment against those who refuse the law—death, exile, confiscation, imprisonment. Swift and serious consequences for rebellion. This reflects how seriously God takes His word and His people's faithfulness to it. We soften this truth sometimes, but ignoring God's law brings real loss.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Blessed be Yahweh, the God of our fathers." Ezra's prayer rises suddenly—praise breaks into the narrative. He recognizes that all this, the king's favor, the resources, the very possibility of rebuilding—it flows from the Lord's hand, not from Persian politics. Gratitude recognizes the true source.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Readers today hear an echo in Ezra's testimony: "I was strengthened according to Yahweh my God's hand on me." We, too, find our strength not in position or wealth but in the Lord's upholding hand. When we set our hearts to seek His law and live it, His hand reaches forward to sustain us. That truth transcends empires and centuries.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
